Staff Report on Consumer Responses to Cigarette Health Information By Bureau of Economics, Federal Trade Commission Published August, 1979 The above-named report presents several! sources which have examined U.S. cigarette smoking behavior in an attempt to track consu- mer response to government health warnings. The report primarily uses government data on pet capita cigarette consumption from 1953 to 1975, and a study conducted by the National Center for Disease Control on the lifetime smoking histories of 12,000 Americans. The authors' ana- lysis makes use of-a statistical projection model designed to isolate the factors which have influenced consumer smoking behavior, and to estimate the degree to which these factors have altered consumption patterns. The report also comments on previous government-sponsored research in this area. The report concludes that, while the government health warning problem has had an effect on U.S. cigarette consumption, the magnitude of this effect is not measurable. This is because the combined effects of various public policy actions and statements (e.g. the Surgeon General's Report of 1964, the anti-smoking advertisements of 1968-1970, the TV advertising ban of 1971) have been both cumulative and gXadual. There is no evidence of a direct consumer response to a particular government action; rather, negative associations have slowly been built up around cigarette smoking which, over time, have caused Americans to alter their smoking patterns. The report is careful, however, to discuaim any proof that consu- mers have responded to the health warnings by rational consideration of the pros and cons of smoking; tfi e study only shows that certain changes have taken place in the cigarette market during the period of the health warnings (after 1964). The authors claim, in fact,, that reports on the success of the anti-smoking advertisements of 1968-1970 were grossly overstated because the method of measurement did' not take into account the residual effects of the 1964 Surgeon General's report, but assumed all changes in smoking habits and attitudes to be a direct, immediate consequence of the commercials. The current study, which takes into account the cumulative effect of all variables over the period under study says that it is impossible to judge the effectiveness of any indi- vidual policy statement, or even if the government'program as a whole was understood and received by the public as intended. This latter ~ point is consistent with Lorillard's own research findings which showed ~ that only a tiny minority of smokers are Immediately influenced by a M government statement (in our case, the Surgeon General's Report issued ~ in January, 1979.) ~j ~d pgNbr=1 In general, the FTC study confirms the judgments and findings of Lorillard's MRD (as reported in the booklet prepared for the five year plan*meeting) concerning the impact of various social and public forces on cigarette use. A summary of the FTC report follows: Summary of Major Findin s 1. Per Capita Consumption Per capita consumption fell at an annul rate of 3.5% betwen 1964 and 1975. However, prediction of post-1963 sales if the government health warnings had not occurred may be "unrealistically high." 2. Tar and Nicotine"Intake Total T&N content of domestic cigarettes has been reduced at an annual rate 01.9% since 1953. This, combined with a decline in consump- tion, has lowered per capita T&N intake by 4.5"0. '::_'Affluent and college-educa,ted smokers tend to smoke products with loucr tar and nicotine levels. The health warnings have been mo:a ~bffectively assimilated by educated people. However, this group also smokes more, a practice which the authors of the report imply reflects , their higher income, but which the tobacco industry would attribute to their use of reduced tar products. (Presumably, if the government study believed that reduced tar and nicotine intake caused smokers to consume more cigarettes, it would diminish the claim that their health warning policy has successfully forced a response from cigarette manufacturers.) 3. Partici ap tion Rate (Number of Smokers) Public policy against cigarette smoking,since 1964 has caused a reduction in the number of smokers (8% by 1975) but not in the consump- tion rate per smoker. In other words, quitting and adoption rates have been affected by government policy, but continuing smokers have not altered their rate of consumption. In particular, quitting has accel- erated among those 46 to 55 years and under 29 years. The FTC also estimates a'"gain" of 8.5% in non-smokers (people who would have started smoking if not for the health warnings), according to their projection model. 4. Adoption Rates Adoption rates among teenagers will determine whether the decline in the number of smokers will continue, or cigarette use will return to for- mer levels. There is not enough data available to make this judgment now; however, data collectedd by the various government studies covered in the report show that teenage smokers have not responded to health warnings. 0 For example: 1) there has been an increase in adoption rates among U1 female teenagers, 2) those starting to smoke after 1964 do not consume ~ C!1 . ~D _ ~ pgNbr=2 fewer cigarettes or smoke brands with lower T&N content than those who started before 1964. (It is doubtful that teenage adoption rates alone -could push cigarette use back up to past levels, since the "'negative" forces tend to cancel out any potential gain: e.g. quit rates among young adult females are very high.) Conclusion The consequence of the health warnings was a reduction in the tar and nicotine content of cigarettes, and a decline in the number of smokers since 1964. There was no effect on the rate of consumption among those who contlnued to smoke. It is not possible to establish a direct link between government policy and consumer behavior, however; other, unmeasured, variables played a part in changing the behavior and preferences of smokers. The actual impact of the health warning pro- gram may even be smaller than estimated in this report. ~,. _.. f: pgNbr=3 </ocr>

A ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit holds that warnings on cigarette packs and in cigarette ads as prescribed by the Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act of 1965 are adequate as a natter of law. Also provided in this section are:    o  Preemption Ruling by the Third U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals    - Petition for Rehearing    - Denial of Rehearing    o  Preemption Ruling by the First U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals    o  Preemption Ruling by the Eleventh U.S.  Circuit Court of Appeals    o  Preemption Ruling by the Sixth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals    o    0) 0)    ro    CD O    '88                                                                                                               Page 1 of 10.3 pgNbr=100 CONGRESSIONAL PREEMPTION AND TOBACCO LITIGATION    A central issue in many of the lawsuits brought against tobacco companies is the question of whether or not the smokers bringing the suits have been adequately warned of the possible risks of smoking cigarettes.    Four separate United States Circuit Courts of Appeal have definitively decided this issue, holding that the Congressionally-mandated warnings on all cigarette packages and advertisements provide an adequate warning. Furthermore, the courts have held that this Congressional action preempts any claims that a smoker made the decision to smoke without adequate information about the potential risks of that choice.    The principal doctrine the courts have used in rejecting an argument of insufficient, warnings is known as Congressional Preemption. Congress passed the 1965 Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act so that consumers would be "adequately informed" about the alleged hazards of smoking. As everyone knows, the means Congress selected for informing consumers is the warning label that is now part of every cigarette package and advertisement. And because Congress determined that the warning is adequate, product liability claims based on the notion that plaintiffs were not adequately warned cannot be upheld.    Clear Intentions    When Congress drafted the Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertising Act, it clearly intended to strike a balance between its concern for the national health policy of smoking education and the protection of the trade and commerce aspects of the tobacco industry. The act came in response to the 1964 Surgeon General's report on cigarette smoking and health, which had already caused some states to pass laws requiring mandatory warning labels for cigarette packages � but the wording of_ each warning was- different.. Realizing the crippling effect a maze' of conflicting state regulations would have on commerce. Congress stepped in to establish a uniform federal program and system of warning labels for cigarettes. The program would assume exclusive jurisdiction over cigarette warnings, advertising and promotional activities, as well as ensure that no state or agency would interfere with cigarette sales. Moreover, Congress intentionally specified that its warning was not only comprehensive but also adequate in terms of informing consumers. No state or municipality could require any further warning. Since 1966, Congress has twice changed the warning language (that exists in Section 1333 of the Act) with the passage of the Public Health Cigarette Smoking Act of 1969 and the 1984 Comprehensive Smoking Education Act. But it has never changed its injunction barring states from requiring additional or different warnings.    Courts Uphold Preemption    Numerous federal and state courts have upheld the Congressional preemption argument in suits brought against cigarette manufacturers.    In the Palmer case (Aug. 15, 1987), the U.S. Court of Appeals for th* First Circuit, in Boston, declared that federal statutes held primacy over state laws and that the federally mandated warning preempts state product liability laws as they relate to tobacco companies. The primary objective of the corporate project is to develop a cigarette of 2 mg tar delivery which has the taste level of a Kent Golden Light. A second corporate objective is to develop a cigarette of 8 mg tar delivery having the taste level of a Marlboro.  It is anticipated that the technology attained in achieving these goals will be broadly applied to the improvements of other brands marketed by the company.    The problems posed by the corporate project have been attacked from several sides by the Sections of Departments assigned to develop the project.  The Product Development Department has concentrated on developing the new product mainly by formulating new blends of tobacco, by modifying cigarette and filter construction, and by testing and evaluating new flavor compositions.  The Research Department, assisted by the Engineering Department, has supported the corporate project by investigating novel ways in which the amount of nicotine delivered relative to tar could be increased so the new products would have an appealing impact to the smoker.    -�'����During the earlier projects the Research Department explored approximately twenty ideas intended to completely or partially achieve the objectives of the corporate project. .This work led to some useful information, but no breakthroughs resulted, instead, a general appreciation of the difficulty of the project was realized.  It became evident that if the Research Department were to accomplish its .mission, process innovations would have to be -c.onfine.d to +he RL manufacturing facility in Danville    PRESENT STATUS OF THE PROBLEM    The present problem before the Research Department is to determine a timely process which can be implemented at Danville to produce an enriched RL sheet useful for incorporation into the 2 rag product.  This sheet should produce flavorful smoke with the needed impact,, yet at the pgNbr=1 - 2 -    same time not produce a tar yield significantly above the sheet presently produced.    The Research Department and the Engineering Department have jointly conducted experiments in Danville during the past four months to produce samples of RL sheet containing supplemental nicotine. These samples have been evaluated by Product Development to determine whether the sheet produced would be useful to the 2 mg project by providing added impact. It was decided that the sheet with supplemental nicotine could not be used since it did not result in a fully balanced product in this particular case.    The limited work at Danville has brought several problems into focus. One longstanding major problem is the poor flavor of the RL sheet presently produced, a flavor which has been characterized as papery and acrid. It has been found that increasing the nicotine content of the RL further increases the acrid qualities of the smoke. This kind of problem has been worked around in the past by compensating these RL negatives with positive contributions from other components of the blend.  It may not be possible to compensate flavor in nicotine augmented RL for use in a 2 mg product because of other limitations.  Therefore, even if a process is devised to produce RL with increased nicotine content to provide impact, it may not be useable until the flavor problems associated with the present RL are solved.
